title: Criticism That Burns: Corrosive, Clever, Wounding, Bracing
core: All four describe criticism sharp enough to hurt, and all four are borrowed from chemistry or the tongue — substances that burn, bite, or pucker. Because the physical metaphors overlap, the words look interchangeable in a sentence about a brutal review. They separate on three questions: whose bitterness is it, is wit required, and does the sentence admire the critic or condemn him.

words.nuance: The bitterness belongs to the **speaker**, not just the line — it attaches to people as readily as to remarks (a caustic ex, a caustic wit). No cleverness required and no accuracy required; it only has to corrode. Of the four, it is the one that most reliably makes the person saying it look damaged.

The only one that requires intelligence. **Mordant** criticism is dry, dark, usually funny, and lands because it is true — you cannot be mordant by shouting or by sheer nastiness. It half-compliments the speaker while flaying the target, which is why satirists and obituarists earn it and bullies never do.

Measures **damage done**, not temperature or wit. It attaches to the attack rather than the attacker — a scathing review, report, rebuke — and it implies the blow actually landed; criticism the target shrugged off is not scathing. Says nothing about whether the critic was clever, only that he was severe and contemptuous.

The one that isn't hot. **Astringent** severity is dry and tightening rather than burning — bracing, medicinal, unsparing without malice, the sting that is supposedly doing you good. Applied to a writer's prose or a critic's judgment it is frequently praise, which none of the others can be.

exam_note: The trap is defaulting to caustic or scathing when the sentence quietly admires the critic — praise for wit points to mordant, praise for bracing dryness to astringent.
